definition: A Classic Maya king or lord; supreme rulers took the title K'uhul Ajaw, meaning holy lord, as messengers between people and gods.
The Maya place-value counting system built on twenties, matching ten fingers and ten toes, written with shells, dots, and bars.
Tropical tree pods whose roasted seeds made frothy spiced royal chocolate drinks and worked as everyday Maya market money.
A deep natural sinkhole in northern Yucatán where collapsed porous limestone exposed cool underground freshwater pools.
The long-nosed Maya god of rain, thunder, and lightning, honoured at caves and cenotes so golden maize crops would thrive.
Great northern Yucatán Maya city built near sacred cenotes, famed for El Castillo step-pyramid, El Caracol observatory, and its Great Ballcourt.
A bottle-shaped underground chamber dug into limestone rock and lined with waterproof lime plaster to store monsoon rainwater.
An independent city and its surrounding farmlands governed by its own ruler, laws, and army, such as Tikal, Palenque, or Copán.
Accordion-folded Maya books made from beaten inner fig-tree bark coated in white lime paste and painted with turkey-quill brushes.
Sweet-smelling tree resin burned by Maya priests inside tall clay censers so fragrant smoke carried prayers up to the gods.
A high narrow Maya stone ceiling built by stepping flat limestone blocks inward from both walls until they met beneath a capstone.
Chopping down wide stretches of forest trees for farmland and plaster kilns, leaving bare hillside soil to wash away in heavy rain.
A long, dangerous stretch of years with far too little rainfall, drying up city reservoirs and withering staple maize harvests.
Round stone astronomical observatory tower at Chichén Itzá whose narrow viewing windows lined up with sunsets and the planet Venus.
The two days each year in spring and autumn when daytime and nighttime last equal hours, casting Kukulkan's serpent shadow at Chichén Itzá.
Over eight hundred carved or painted Maya hieroglyphic signs standing for whole words or spoken syllables to spell complete sentences.
The 365-day Maya solar farming calendar that guided maize planting and harvests alongside the 260-day sacred Tzolk'in calendar.
A traditional Maya tunic or blouse hand-woven on a portable backstrap loom with colourful geometric patterns unique to each town.
Tough, shining green stone prized above gold by Maya royals for masks, collars, and earflares symbolising breath and young maize.
The mighty Maya feathered serpent god of wind, rain, and learning, honoured on Chichén Itzá's 365-step El Castillo pyramid.
Sacred Mesoamerican corn soaked in limewater and ground into nourishing tortilla dough as the staple food of every Maya city.
The historical region stretching from southern Mexico through Guatemala, Belize, Honduras, and El Salvador where Maya cities flourished.
A flat three-legged or curved volcanic grinding stone used every dawn with a stone roller to crush soaked maize into fresh dough.
Glossy jet-black volcanic glass mined in the southern highlands and flaked into blades and spear points sharper than steel.
The fast sacred Maya ballgame where padded players bounced a heavy solid rubber ball off their hips inside sloping stone courts.
The sacred K'iche' Maya creation book telling how the gods shaped humans from maize dough and how the Hero Twins outwitted Xibalba.
Tall upright limestone slabs carved with royal portraits and hieroglyphic dates recording the births and victories of Maya rulers.
The 260-day sacred Maya ritual calendar that meshed like a cogwheel with the 365-day solar Haab' once every fifty-two years.
